transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2027-06-09   Start: 15:00 UTC   Duration: ~48m
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Rojas (Redwood SE), Priya Shah (LumenHealth Platform), Tom Erickson (Lumen SRE), Jules Martin (Security), Aaron Lee (Network), Nina Gomez (PM)

Summary:
Quick rundown of tenant isolation strategy for private VPC deployment, walking through egress bridge / shared NAT patterns, PrivateLink alternatives, DNS resolver placement, and runtime-level impacts on KV cache and batching. Agreed to run a lab for KV-cache hit profiling and a NAT hairpin test in a staging VPC.

Topics covered:
- Tenant isolation patterns (C shared egress vs. per-tenant NAT)
- PrivateLink vs. cross-account peering for inference control plane
- DNS resolver placement and split-horizon effects on KV cache hits
- KV cache behavior under hairpinned egress and NAT translation
- Batching and quantization implications for latency and throughput
- Fallbacks: hosted vs dedicated in mixed connectivity environments

Action items (recorded in discussion):
- See metadata action_items for owners/due-dates.

Transcript body:
[00:00:00] Maya Chen: alright everyone good afternoon thanks for joining, we're gonna kick off, um, hi i'm Maya from Redwood, AE on the account, with Diego our SE, we'll drive today's workshop around tenant isolation and the egress bridge pattern.
[00:00:28] Priya Shah: hi all thanks, we've got a couple of engineers on the line, hope to get down to specifics — NAT counts, routing table per-tenant, and see how K V cache behaves when traffic is hairpinned back through our egress.
[00:00:47] Diego Rojas: cool, quick agenda, we'll sketch three topologies: shared egress (central NAT), per-tenant NAT, and privatelink-proxy. We'll then map latency implications to KV cache and batching.
[00:01:12] Tom Erickson: quick note — our primary constraint is compliance: tenant isolation at L2/L3 and audit trails. We need to avoid cross-tenant leakage and keep flow logs.
[00:01:35] Jules Martin: on security side we also want KMS/HSM integration and proof of no data egress to internet for PII workloads.
[00:01:50] Maya Chen: totally. we'll point out where the runtime does encryption at rest and where network egress touches those boundaries.
[00:02:20] Aaron Lee: question up front, do we have a preference for PrivateLink versus cross-account peering? Peering is cheaper but harder to manage multi-AZ.
[00:02:42] Diego Rojas: Peering is fine for symmetric routing but PrivateLink gives you endpoint-level control and avoids exposing route tables. The trade is TLS termination and SNI at the endpoint which affects MTU and thus payload fragmentation — that in turn affects KV cache payload sizes.
[00:03:10] Nina Gomez: could you explain that MTU thing again — we saw 1500 to 9000 differences in our testing.
[00:03:34] Diego Rojas: sure — when you run through privatelink/privatelinkish proxies you introduce extra headers and potential encapsulation, path MTU can drop; smaller MTU increases fragmentation and can increase per-token serialization overhead. In practice we recommend a baseline MTU 1400+ on the bridge to avoid fragmentation at typical request sizes.
[00:04:05] [00:04:05] Priya Shah: noted, we'll check our transit MTU.
[00:04:30] Maya Chen: sketching the topologies now — shared egress: many tenants route to a central NAT/gateway. pros: less NAT gateway scale, predictable routing; cons: single blast radius, KV cache namespace collisions unless runtime namespaces tenants.
[00:04:55] Tom Erickson: do you mean the runtime has tenant-aware KV cache? we thought the cache key was model+prefix hash only.
[00:05:15] Diego Rojas: good call — runtime supports tenant-scoped cache keys, it's configurable. by default we scope by tenant-id + model + prompt prefix. but if traffic is hairpinned through a single NAT and we strip source IP, you need to pass tenant header or token to keep cache contexts correct.
[00:05:45] Jules Martin: so passing tenant-id in header is mandatory for shared egress? any risk of header spoofing?
[00:06:05] Diego Rojas: header is OK if you're doing mTLS or PrivateLink with IAM principals; otherwise use a signed request header. We'll share a sample signed header implementation.
[00:06:30] [00:06:30] Aaron Lee: about DNS — we run split-horizon resolvers in each AZ. How does that affect connection reuse?
[00:06:50] Diego Rojas: split-horizon can cause hostnames to resolve to different IPs causing multiple TCP/TLS sessions to the same logical endpoint — that increases cold-starts for KV cache since sessions and their associated persistent connections are per IP. Ideally keep resolver responses consistent for inference endpoints so the runtime sees stable backends and reuses persistent connections.
[00:07:18] Priya Shah: that matches our logs — we see intermittent p99 spikes correlated with resolver TTL expirations.
[00:07:30] Maya Chen: two mitigations: lower TTLs plus client side connection pooling tuned in the runtime; or centralized resolver with anycast in front of AZ resolvers. Both have tradeoffs.
[00:07:58] Tom Erickson: on NAT scaling — we have bursty traffic, does Redwood recommend many small NAT gateways or a small number of big ones?
[00:08:16] Diego Rojas: architecturally we like at least two NAT GW per AZ for HA. For burst smoothing, combine per-tenant token bucket rate limits at the edge with a central egress that can autoscale. Note: lots of concurrent short-lived TLS sessions will hurt throughput due to TLS handshakes which interacts poorly with small batching.
[00:08:45] [00:08:45] Priya Shah: can we talk KV cache behavior when requests are multiplexed across proxies?
[00:09:00] Diego Rojas: yes — if the runtime sees requests from multiple proxies that don't carry tenant context in the same way, you'll see lower hit rates. Also KV cache locality matters: we do local KV caches per worker with optional pinned shared cache via in-memory coordination. If your network routing causes requests to land on different workers frequently you'll lose temporal locality.
[00:09:30] Maya Chen: short example — with 8 worker shards and round robin LB, a long conversation that alternates connections can keep missing the local KV cache. The runtime supports sticky sessions (session affinity) to keep KV locality.
[00:09:55] Tom Erickson: sticky sessions concern me for scale; doesn't that reduce ability to spread load?
[00:10:08] Diego Rojas: it's a trade. For low-latency chat flows you often prefer affinity with KV locality; for high throughput stateless generative batches you prefer round robin. We usually recommend dynamic affinity: stick for conversation tasks, round-robin for batched inference.
[00:10:35] [00:10:35] Priya Shah: what's the impact of quantization here? does int8 change packet sizes or memory movement?
[00:10:52] Diego Rojas: quant changes compute/IO patterns more than network packet sizes. INT8/4 reduces memory bandwith per token and reduces latency per token on the GPU, meaning sequenced requests finish faster and KV cache gets hit more often per second. But watch batch sizes: quantized kernels often prefer slightly larger micro-batches to amortize setup. So your latency SLO vs cost mix shifts.
[00:11:25] Maya Chen: Diego's point — small batches + quant can be worse p50 but better cost; larger batches give better throughput. We'll show simulations.
[00:11:48] [00:11:48] Aaron Lee: we have an egress firewall that NATs and does DPI, it rewrites some headers. Any known issues with DPI and the runtime?
[00:12:05] Diego Rojas: DPI can break keep-alive and HTTP/2 multiplexing if it acts as a proxy changing semantics. Runtime prefers HTTP/2 or persistent HTTP/1.1 connections to reduce per-request overhead. If firewall terminates TLS, ensure it propagates original SNI/client cert info in headers for tenant scoping.
[00:12:34] Jules Martin: firewall termination is a no-go for some workloads.
[00:12:44] Maya Chen: understood. we can architect for both: a PrivateLink path (no TLS termination) for sensitive tenants and an inspected path for others.
[00:12:58] [00:12:58] Priya Shah: can we deep-dive on hairpinning? we suspect some of our traffic leaves az and comes back and that adds 50–120ms occasionally.
[00:13:18] Diego Rojas: hairpinning increases RTT and also can flip source IPs which if used for affinity breaks KV locality. For example, a request from user session A goes to LB-A, egresses through NAT1 and then back to a different LB-B in another AZ and lands on worker shard 5 instead of 2. That's two levels of broken locality. Solutions: keep regional egress in the same AZ as the worker group, or retain tenant metadata across hops.
[00:13:52] Tom Erickson: is there a recommended way to pass tenant metadata securely?
[00:14:05] Diego Rojas: signed JWT in a custom header or mTLS with client cert mapped to tenant. We prefer mTLS for internal RPC; signed headers are fine across boundary where mTLS isn't possible.
[00:14:26] [00:14:26] Maya Chen: demo time — Diego, can you walk through the perf numbers from our staging lab?
[00:14:36] Diego Rojas: sure — i'll summarize: scenario A (per-tenant NAT, stickiness): p50=45ms p95=110ms, KV hit rate 78%. Scenario B (shared NAT, no tenant header, round-robin): p50=62ms p95=220ms, KV hit 37%. Scenario C (PrivateLink + mTLS): p50=48ms p95=120ms, KV hit 74% — PrivateLink was slightly higher CPU per request due to TLS termination overhead at endpoint but it preserved tenant scoping so higher cache hits.
[00:15:10] Priya Shah: those numbers align with our expectations. Can you show the test harness?
[00:15:20] Diego Rojas: yes deck + perf spreadsheet link: https://drive.redwood/reports/lumen-kvcache-lab (note: placeholder, we'll upload the real sheet).
[00:15:40] [00:15:40] Aaron Lee: curious about connection reuse counts — what's the recommended keepalive settings?
[00:15:55] Diego Rojas: runtime default is keepalive=90s and connection pooling per-worker up to 128 connections. For your workload with many small requests, bump keepalive to 120s and increase max pooled connections to 256 in the edge proxies.
[00:16:20] Maya Chen: also instrument idle connection metrics so you can tune.
[00:16:38] [00:16:38] Tom Erickson: we also need to think about per-tenant logging and flow logs for audit — how does Redwood expose per-request metadata?
[00:16:54] Maya Chen: we emit per-request tracing at token-level optionally to your log collector (GCP/CloudWatch/Splunk). For privacy, you can redact prompt text and only keep hashes and request metadata. We can ship a sample Fluent Bit config.
[00:17:20] Jules Martin: good. show me how we prove no data egress to public internet for those tenants.
[00:17:33] Diego Rojas: for Private deployments we run the control plane in your VPC or via PrivateLink; attachments are over mTLS and there's an optional data-plane path where models and KV never leave your network. We'll provide an architecture doc with audit checkpoints.
[00:17:58] [00:17:58] Priya Shah: on retries — we have aggressive retries at the CDN layer which can create duplicate requests and pollute KV counts. Any mitigation?
[00:18:15] Diego Rojas: add idempotency tokens at the request level; runtime will dedupe based on token within a short window. Also backoff jitter to avoid thundering herd to the cache.
[00:18:36] Maya Chen: quick pause — any other infra constraints you want us to address before we move into lab planning?
[00:18:49] Nina Gomez: we need to confirm whether we can run the lab in our staging account with privatelink endpoints or if Redwood needs to spin up a test VPC.
[00:19:02] Diego Rojas: we can support both. for full-fidelity network tests we prefer your staging VPC so NAT/GW/MTU and firewall behavior are real. If that's not possible, we can emulate hairpin and DNS TTLs in a Redwood test VPC.
[00:19:26] [00:19:26] Priya Shah: we'll try staging first.
[00:19:36] Tom Erickson: about quotas — if we put many tenants on a shared egress, how do you ensure noisy neighbor protection?
[00:19:54] Diego Rojas: we support per-tenant rate limiting, token-level circuit breakers, and route policies to throttle heavy tenants to a lower capacity tier. Also auto fallback to a cheaper model variant if a tenant exceeds cost threshold.
[00:20:15] Maya Chen: that ties into Redwood Optimize — we can suggest quantization profiles and batching settings per-tenant to control unit cost.
[00:20:37] [00:20:37] Priya Shah: what about SNI routing with PrivateLink — do you recommend multiple endpoints per tenant or a shared endpoint with header-based routing?
[00:20:53] Diego Rojas: multiple endpoints gives stronger network isolation but is more operationally heavy. Shared endpoint with mTLS client certs and header validation is a common compromise.
[00:21:15] Aaron Lee: does PrivateLink preserve original client source IP?
[00:21:30] Diego Rojas: no, PrivateLink terminates at the endpoint; you get the endpoint's IP. You need to rely on client certs or headers rather than source IP for tenant identity.
[00:21:46] [00:21:46] Tom Erickson: any gotchas with S3 egress for model downloads in this topology?
[00:21:58] Diego Rojas: if your S3 access is via a NAT that rewrites sources, you'll need appropriate bucket policies keyed to the NAT role. Also consider using VPC endpoints for S3 to avoid egress. Model downloads are one-time but can be large; plan for warm caches on nodes and validate SHAS.
[00:22:24] Priya Shah: about KV cache warmup — any recommended warmup policy for high-latency tenants?
[00:22:36] Diego Rojas: pre-warm cache with representative prompts off-peak, or use an LRU-prefetch with prefix matching. For chat use case, keep last N session prefixes pinned. We can show scripts.
[00:22:58] [00:22:58] Maya Chen: back to batching — what's your recommended batching strategy for mixed short and long requests?
[00:23:10] Diego Rojas: hybrid: separate small-latency queue (max batch 4, aggressive flush at 30ms) and a throughput queue (max batch 32, wait 100ms). Runtime supports dynamic routing by request-class header.
[00:23:36] Tom Erickson: how do we classify requests? by token budget in the header?
[00:23:47] Diego Rojas: yes token estimate header or client-side hint works well. The runtime will also auto-detect sequence length patterns.
[00:24:08] [00:24:08] Priya Shah: are there monitoring hooks for KV cache health and batching efficiency?
[00:24:20] Maya Chen: yes — per-route metrics: cache hit rate (by tenant), miss latency, batch size histograms, GPU utilization, and wasted cycles due to thin batches. We'll provide a Grafana dashboard template.
[00:24:45] Diego Rojas: also trace per-request path so you can correlate a p95 token latency with DNS lookups, NAT hops, and cache misses.
[00:25:06] [00:25:06] Aaron Lee: can we schedule the lab to include a NAT hairpin test where we intentionally route a subset of traffic through a different AZ NAT?
[00:25:18] Maya Chen: yes, that's in the proposed lab. We'll coordinate with Priya/Tom to pick a workload sample and run three topologies with KV instrumentation.
[00:25:36] Priya Shah: we'll gather the sample. Expect 1–2 hours of test runs.
[00:25:46] [00:25:46] Diego Rojas: one more note — DNS resolver TLS (DoT) can add ~10ms on first connect; if your resolvers use DoT make sure persistent connections are enabled to avoid per-request overhead.
[00:26:06] Maya Chen: good call.
[00:26:18] [00:26:18] Tom Erickson: any known anomalies when running quantized models in on-prem with lower NIC speeds?
[00:26:32] Diego Rojas: network becomes more dominant when quant reduces compute. If your NIC is <25Gbps and you're doing lots of small requests, you might be compute-starved in a different way; watch CPU and NIC saturation, and consider pinning models to GPUs that have local NVMe caches to reduce network model fetches.
[00:26:58] Priya Shah: how does Redwood handle model version pinning during rollouts in Private VPC?
[00:27:12] Maya Chen: rollouts are controlled via the control plane; for Private deployments we support canary routing where a percent of traffic routes to new model artifact via routing policy. We'll coordinate with your release window to sync model caches.
[00:27:36] [00:27:36] Nina Gomez: we need a checklist to show our security team.
[00:27:46] Maya Chen: we'll send the security pack (SOC2 summary, network checklist, sample RBAC, KMS integration doc).
[00:27:57] [00:27:57] Diego Rojas: also including the perf spreadsheet and the test harness repo link.
[00:28:10] Priya Shah: sounds good. one last question — do you support token-level cost allocation per tenant?
[00:28:24] Maya Chen: yes, we have token attribution and per-tenant cost reports in Redwood Console — you can map keys or tenant ids to billing units.
[00:28:38] [00:28:38] Tom Erickson: ok let's recap and finalize next steps.
[00:28:45] Maya Chen: recap: Redwood to share topology sketch, perf sheet, security pack; Lumen to provide staging VPC access or exports, NAT counts, MTU and a representative traffic sample. We'll schedule a 2-hour lab next week to run KV-cache hairpin tests.
[00:29:10] Priya Shah: agreed. expect the sample and CIDRs by 2027-06-11.
[00:29:20] Julia Martin [sic]: (Jules) thanks all, looking forward to the security doc.
[00:29:32] Maya Chen: thanks everyone, we'll follow up in CRM with invites and links.

End of transcript.
